newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbs have cautious hopes of opposition rule.
newsitem.headline: Serbs have cautious hopes of opposition rule.

text.p: A minority of Serbs believe the opposition would improve their economy or political freedoms and half fear the ruling socialists will never relinquish power peacefully, an opinion poll said on Saturday.

The findings were published by the independent daily Nasa Borba ahead of a Serbian parliament session which is expected to endorse election victories by the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition in Belgrade and other disputed towns.

Recognition of the results after 81 days of street protests will hand Zajedno control of 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest towns, ending half a century of unbroken rule by the ex-communist Socialist party (SPS).
It will also provide the three Zajedno parties with a springboard to challenge SPS supremacy in presidential and parliamentary elections due by the end of the year.
The poll of 2,040 voters by the Belgrade Social Sciences Institute showed 51 percent doubted the SPS would leave power without a struggle if defeated. Only 21 percent believed in a peaceful handover.
Twentynine percent thought Zajedno - which contains only one small party committed to recognisable Western-style democracy - could win national elections.
The SPS and its allies won a landslide in federal parliament elections last November at the same time as it attemped to rig the municipal elections against Zajedno.
The poll said 40 percent of voters thought Zajedno would take revenge on the SPS if it won power but only 23 percent feared chaos and civil war.
Around a third thought that a transfer of power was important or that economic revival and greater political freedom were likely under Zajedno.
Milosevic asked the government this week after a long battle between SPS hardliners and pragmatists to rush a law through parliament recognising the socialist defeats.
The session is due on Tuesday but Zajedno has maintained its street pressure, sceptical after being cheated and misled in the past that Milosevic will deliver all he has promised.

International law expert Vojin Dimitrijevic warned that the election law, a one-off devised for the occasion, could face a successful challenge in the constitutional court once the streets were cleared.
Milosevic, fighting for his own political survival, ceded the elections after violence in Belgrade last Sunday when riot police clubbed peaceful demonstrators and turned water cannon on them.
A fair settlement of the dispute would enable Serbia's gradual return to international diplomatic and financial bodies if accompanied by political reforms demanded by Zajedno and the West.

But SPS hardliners who fear reform would destroy their grip on power and resisted allowing the opposition to take control of the big towns will watch the process carefully and could still intervene against it in the coming months, diplomats have warned.
They could either force Milosevic to side with them or oust him to ensure continued SPS supremacy.
